entries.8ccb1761ebcfdcfce6fe739515eca262eac0fc20: <div sID="gen17976" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="36" osisID="Jer.36" sID="Jer.36"/> <div eID="gen17976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17977" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17978" type="x-p"/> Here is another expedient tried to work upon this heedless and untoward people, but it is tried in vain. A roll of a book is provided, containing an abstract or abridgment of all the sermons that Jeremiah had preached to them, that they might be put in mind of what they had heard and might the better understand it, when they had it all before them at one view. Now here we have, I. The writing of this roll by Baruch, as Jeremiah dictated it, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.1-Jer.36.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. The reading of the roll by Baruch to all the people publicly on a fast-day (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.5-Jer.36.10">ver. 5-10</reference>), afterwards by Baruch to the princes privately (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.11-Jer.36.19">ver. 11-19</reference>), and lastly by Jehudi to the king, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.20-Jer.36.21">ver. 20, 21</reference>. III. The burning of the roll by the king, with orders to prosecute Jeremiah and Baruch, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.22-Jer.36.26">ver. 22-26</reference>. IV. The writing of another roll, with large additions, particularly of Jehoiakim's doom for burning the former, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.27-Jer.36.32">ver. 27-32</reference>.
entries.308bbc516f0506b00ed871e6949e2ba8ca526649: <div eID="gen17978" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17977" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Roll Written by Baruch. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 607.)</title> <div sID="gen17979" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, <hi type="italic">that</hi> this word came unto Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Take thee a roll of a book, and write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spake unto thee, from the days of Josiah, even unto this day. <hi type="super">3</hi> It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I purpose to do unto them; that they may return every man from his evil way; that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah: and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book. <hi type="super">5</hi> And Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> shut up; I cannot go into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore go thou, and read in the roll, which thou hast written from my mouth, the words of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the ears of the people in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house upon the fasting day: and also thou shalt read them in the ears of all Judah that come out of their cities. <hi type="super">7</hi> It may be they will present their supplication before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and will return every one from his evil way: for great <hi type="italic">is</hi> the anger and the fury that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath pronounced against this people. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book the words of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house. <div eID="gen17979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17980" type="x-p"/> In the beginning of Ezekiel's prophecy we meet with <hi type="italic">a roll</hi> written <hi type="italic">in vision,</hi> for discovery of the things therein contained to the prophet himself, who was to receive and digest them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.9-Ezek.2.10">Ezek. ii. 9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.1">iii. 1</reference>. Here, in the latter end of Jeremiah's prophecy, we meet with <hi type="italic">a roll</hi> written <hi type="italic">in fact,</hi> for discovery of the things contained therein to the people, who were to hear and give heed to them; for the written word and other good books are of great use both to ministers and people. We have here, <div eID="gen17980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17981" type="x-p"/> I. The command which God gave to Jeremiah to write a summary of his sermons, of all the reproofs and all the warnings he had given in God's name to his people, ever since he first began to be a preacher, in the thirteenth year of Josiah, <hi type="italic">to this day,</hi> which was in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.2-Jer.36.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. What had been only spoken must now be written, that it might be reviewed, and that it might spread the further and last the longer. What had been spoken at large, with frequent repetitions of the same things, perhaps in the same words (which has its advantage one way), must now be contracted and put into less compass, that the several parts of it might be better compared together, which has its advantage another way. What they had heard once must be recapitulated, and rehearsed to them again, that what was forgotten might be called to mind again and what made no impression upon them at the first hearing might take hold of them when they heard it the second time. And what was perhaps already written, and published in single sermons, must be collected into one volume, that none might be lost. Note, The writing of the scripture is by divine appointment. And observe the reason here given for the writing of this roll (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">It may be the house of Judah will hear.</hi> Not that the divine prescience was at any uncertainty concerning the event: with that there is no peradventure; God knew certainly <hi type="italic">that they would deal very treacherously,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa. xlviii. 8</reference>. But the divine wisdom directed to this as a proper means for attaining the desired end: and, if it failed, they would be the more inexcusable. And, though God foresaw that they would not hear, he did not tell the prophet so, but prescribed this method to him as a probably one to be used, in the hopes that they would <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> that is, heed and regard what they heard, take notice of it and mix faith with it: for otherwise our hearing the word, though an angel from heaven were to read or preach it to us, would stand us in no stead. Now observe here, 1. What it is hoped they will thus hear: <hi type="italic">All that evil which I purpose to do unto them.</hi> Note, The serious consideration of the certain fatal consequences of sin will be of great use to us to bring us to God. 2. What it is hoped will be produced thereby: <hi type="italic">They will hear, that they may return every man from his evil way.</hi> Note, The conversion of sinners from their evil courses is that which ministers should aim at in preaching; and people hear the word in vain if that point be not gained with them. To what purpose do we hear of the evil God will bring upon us for sin if we continue, notwithstanding, to do evil against him? 3. Of what vast advantage their consideration and conversion will be to them: <hi type="italic">That I may forgive their iniquity.</hi> This plainly implies the honour of God's justice, with which it is not consistent that he should forgive the sin unless the sinner repent of it and turn from it; but it plainly expresses the honour of his mercy, that he is very ready to forgive sin and only waits till the sinner be qualified to receive forgiveness, and therefore uses various means to bring us to repentance, <hi type="italic">that he may forgive.</hi> <div eID="gen17981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17982" type="x-p"/> II. The instructions which Jeremiah gave to Baruch his scribe, pursuant to the command he had received from God, and the writing of the roll accordingly, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.4">v. 4</reference>. God bade Jeremiah write, but, it should seem, he had not the <hi type="italic">pen of a ready writer,</hi> he could not write fast, or fair, so as Baruch could, and therefore he made use of him as his amanuensis. St. Paul wrote but few of his epistles with his own hand, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.11">Gal. vi. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.22">Rom. xvi. 22</reference>. God dispenses his gifts variously; some have a good faculty at speaking, others at writing, and neither can say to the other, We have <hi type="italic">no need of you,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.21">1 Cor. xii. 21</reference>. The Spirit of God dictated to Jeremiah, and he to Baruch, who had been employed by Jeremiah as trustee for him in his purchase of the field (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.12">ch. xxxii. 12</reference>) and now was advanced to be his scribe and substitute in his prophetical office; and, if we may credit the apocryphal book that bears his name, he was afterwards himself a prophet to the captives in Babylon. Those that begin low are likely to rise high, and it is good for those that are designed for prophets to have their education under prophets and to be serviceable to them. Baruch wrote what Jeremiah dictated in a <hi type="italic">roll of a book</hi> on pieces of parchment, or vellum, which were joined together, the top of one to the bottom of the other, so making one long scroll, which was rolled perhaps upon a staff. <div eID="gen17982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17983" type="x-p"/> III. The orders which Jeremiah gave to Baruch to read what he had written to the people. Jeremiah, it seems was <hi type="italic">shut up,</hi> and <hi type="italic">could not go to the house of the Lord</hi> himself, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.5">v. 5</reference>. Though he was not a close prisoner, for then there would have been no occasion to send officers to seize him (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.26">v. 26</reference>), yet he was forbidden by the king to appear in the temple, was shut out thence where he might be serving God and doing good, which was as bad to him as if he had been shut up in a dungeon. Jehoiakim was ripening apace for ruin when he thus silenced God's faithful messengers. But, when Jeremiah could not go to the temple himself, he sent one that was deputed by him to read to the people what he would himself have said. Thus St. Paul wrote epistles to the churches which he could not visit in person. Nay, it was what he himself had often said to them. Note, The writing and repeating of the sermons that have been preached may contribute very much towards the answering of the great ends of preaching. What we have heard and known it is good for us to hear again, that we may know it better. To preach and write the same thing is safe and profitable, and many times very necessary (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.1">Phil. iii. 1</reference>), and we must be glad to hear a good word from God, though we have it, as here, at second hand. Both ministers and people must do what they can when they cannot do what they would. Observe, When God ordered the reading of the roll he said, <hi type="italic">It may be they will hear and return from their evil ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.36.3">v. 3</reference>. When Jeremiah orders it, he says, <hi type="italic">It may be they will pray</hi> (they will <hi type="italic">present their supplications before the Lord</hi>) and will <hi type="italic">return from their evil way.</hi> Note, Prayer to God for grace to turn us is necessary in order to our turning; and those that are convinced by the word of God of the necessity of returning to him will present their supplications to him for that grace. And the consideration of this, that <hi type="italic">great is the anger which God has pronounced against us</hi> for sin, should quicken both our prayers and our endeavours. Now, according to these orders, Baruch did read <hi type="italic">out of the book the words of the Lord,</hi> whenever there was a <hi type="italic">holy convocation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.36.8">v. 8</reference>.
entries.1b3af7d484f3437848bab99ed943ca3fd260a3bd: <div eID="gen17983" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Baruch Reads the Roll to the Princes. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 607.)</title> <div sID="gen17984" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And it came to pass in the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, in the ninth month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> they proclaimed a fast before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to all the people in Jerusalem, and to all the people that came from the cities of Judah unto Jerusalem. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then read Baruch in the book the words of Jeremiah in the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe, in the higher court, at the entry of the new gate of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house, in the ears of all the people. <hi type="super">11</hi> When Michaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, had heard out of the book all the words of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="super">12</hi> Then he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, <hi type="italic">even</hi> Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Achbor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then Michaiah declared unto them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the book in the ears of the people. <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, unto Baruch, saying, Take in thine hand the roll wherein thou hast read in the ears of the people, and come. So Baruch the son of Neriah took the roll in his hand, and came unto them. <hi type="super">15</hi> And they said unto him, Sit down now, and read it in our ears. So Baruch read <hi type="italic">it</hi> in their ears. <hi type="super">16</hi> Now it came to pass, when they had heard all the words, they were afraid both one and other, and said unto Baruch, We will surely tell the king of all these words. <hi type="super">17</hi> And they asked Baruch, saying, Tell us now, How didst thou write all these words at his mouth? <hi type="super">18</hi> Then Baruch answered them, He pronounced all these words unto me with his mouth, and I wrote <hi type="italic">them</hi> with ink in the book. <hi type="super">19</hi> Then said the princes unto Baruch, Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah; and let no man know where ye be. <div eID="gen17984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17985" type="x-p"/> It should seem that Baruch had been frequently reading out of the book, to all companies that would give him the hearing, before the most solemn reading of it altogether which is here spoken of; for the directions were given about it in the <hi type="italic">fourth year of Jehoiakim,</hi> whereas this was done <hi type="italic">in the fifth year,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">v. 9</reference>. But some think that the writing of the book fairly over took up so much time that it was another year ere it was perfected; and yet perhaps it might not be past a month or two; he might begin in the latter end of the fourth year and finish it in the beginning of the fifth, for <hi type="italic">thee ninth month</hi> refers to the computation of the year in general, not to the year of that reign. Now observe here, 1. The government appointed a public fast to be religiously observed (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">v. 9</reference>), on account either of the distress they were brought into by the army of the Chaldeans or of the want of rain (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.1">ch. xiv. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">They proclaimed a fast to the people;</hi> whether the king and princes or the priests, ordered this fast, is not certain; but it was plain that God by his providence called them aloud to it. Note, Great shows of piety and devotion may be found even among those who, though they keep up these <hi type="italic">forms of godliness,</hi> are strangers and enemies to <hi type="italic">the power</hi> of it. But what will such hypocritical services avail? Fasting, without reforming and turning away from sin, will never turn away the judgments of God, <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.10">Jon. iii. 10</reference>. Notwithstanding this fast, God proceeded in his controversy with this people. 2. Baruch repeated Jeremiah's sermons publicly in the house of the Lord, on the fast-day. He stood in a chamber that belonged to Gemariah, and out of a window, or balcony, read to the people that were in the court, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.10">v. 10</reference>. Note, When we are speaking to God we must be willing to hear from him; and therefore, on days of fasting and prayer, it is requisite that the word be read and preached. <hi type="italic">Hearken unto me, that God may hearken unto you.</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.9.7">Judg. ix. 7</reference>. For our help in suing out mercy and grace, it is proper that we should be told of sin and duty. 3. An account was brought of this to the princes that attended the court and were now together in the secretary's office, here called <hi type="italic">the scribe's chamber,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.36.12">v. 12</reference>. It should seem, though the princes had called the people to meet in the house of God, to fact, and pray, and hear the word, they did not think fit to attend there themselves, which was a sign that it was not from a principle of true devotion, but merely for fashion sake, that they proclaimed this fast. We are willing to hope that it was not with a bad design, to bring Jeremiah into trouble for his preaching, but with a good design, to bring the princes into trouble for their sins, that Michaiah informed the princes of what Baruch had read; for his father Gemariah so far countenanced Baruch as to lend him his chamber to read out of. Michaiah finds the princes sitting in <hi type="italic">the scribe's chamber,</hi> and tells them they had better have been where he had been, hearing a good sermon in the temple, which he gives them the heads of. Note, When we have heard some good word that has affected and edified us we should be ready to communicate it to others that did not hear it, for their edification. <hi type="italic">Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.</hi> 4. Baruch is sent for, and is ordered to sit down among them and read it all over again to them (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.14-Jer.36.15">v. 14, 15</reference>), which he readily did, not complaining that he was weary with his public work and therefore desiring to be excused, nor upbraiding the princes with their being absent from the temple, where they might have heard it when he read it there. Note, God's ministers must <hi type="italic">become all things to all men, if by any means they may gain some,</hi> must comply with them in circumstances, that they may secure the substance. St. Paul preached privately to those of reputation, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.2">Gal. ii. 2</reference>. 5. The princes were for the present much affected with the word that was read to them, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.16">v. 16</reference>. Observe, <hi type="italic">They heard all the words</hi> they did not interrupt him, but very patiently attended to the reading of the whole book; for otherwise how could they form a competent judgment of it? And, <hi type="italic">when they had heard all, they were afraid,</hi> were all afraid, <hi type="italic">one</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">another;</hi> like Felix, who trembled at Paul's reasonings. The reproofs were just, the threatenings terrible, and the predictions now in a fair way to be fulfilled; so that, laying all together, they were in a great consternation. We are not told what impressions this reading of the roll made upon the people (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.10">v. 10</reference>), but the princes were put into a fright by it, and (as some read it) <hi type="italic">looked one upon another,</hi> not knowing what to say. They were all convinced that it was worthy to be regarded, but none of them had courage to second it, only they agreed to <hi type="italic">tell the king of all these words;</hi> and, if he think fit to give credit to them, they will, otherwise not, no, though it were to prevent the ruin of the nation. And yet at the same time they knew the king's mind so far that they advised Baruch and Jeremiah to hide themselves (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.19">v. 19</reference>) and to shift as they could for their own safety, expecting no other than that the king, instead of being convinced, would be exasperated. Note, It is common for sinners, under convictions, to endeavour to shake them off, by shifting off the prosecution of them to other persons, as these princes here, or to another <hi type="italic">more convenient season,</hi> as Felix. 6. They asked Baruch a trifling question, <hi type="italic">How he wrote all these words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.17">v. 17</reference>), as if they suspected there was something extraordinary in it; but Baruch gives them a plain answer, that there was nothing but what was common in the manner of the writing—Jeremiah dictated and he wrote, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.18">v. 18</reference>. But thus it is common for those who would avoid the convictions of the word of God to start needless questions about the way and manner of the inspiration of it.
entries.754624900238500d9d319649806c9ee6d5f78298: <div eID="gen17985" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah's Roll Consumed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 607.)</title> <div sID="gen17986" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> And they went in to the king into the court, but they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, and told all the words in the ears of the king. <hi type="super">21</hi> So the king sent Jehudi to fetch the roll: and he took it out of Elishama the scribe's chamber. And Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes which stood beside the king. <hi type="super">22</hi> Now the king sat in the winter house in the ninth month: and <hi type="italic">there was a fire</hi> on the hearth burning before him. <hi type="super">23</hi> And it came to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the fire that <hi type="italic">was</hi> on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that <hi type="italic">was</hi> on the hearth. <hi type="super">24</hi> Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments, <hi type="italic">neither</hi> the king, nor any of his servants that heard all these words. <hi type="super">25</hi> Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them. <hi type="super">26</hi> But the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hid them. <hi type="super">27</hi> Then the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came to Jeremiah, after that the king had burned the roll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah, saying, <hi type="super">28</hi> Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned. <hi type="super">29</hi> And thou shalt say to Jehoiakim king of Judah, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Thou hast burned this roll, saying, Why hast thou written therein, saying, The king of Babylon shall certainly come and destroy this land, and shall cause to cease from thence man and beast? <hi type="super">30</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of Jehoiakim king of Judah; He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David: and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost. <hi type="super">31</hi> And I will punish him and his seed and his servants for their iniquity; and I will bring upon them, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and upon the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them; but they hearkened not. <hi type="super">32</hi> Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words. <div eID="gen17986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17987" type="x-p"/> We have traced the roll to the people, and to the princes, and here we are to follow it to the king; and we find, <div eID="gen17987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17988" type="x-p"/> I. That, upon notice given him concerning it, he sent for it, and ordered it to be read to him, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.20-Jer.36.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. He did not desire that Baruch would come and read it himself, who could read it more intelligently and with more authority and affection than any one else; nor did he order one of his princes to do it (though it would have been no disparagement to the greatest of them), much less would he vouchsafe to read it himself; but Jehudi, one of his pages now in waiting, who was sent to fetch it, is bidden to read it, who perhaps scarcely knew how to make sense of it. But those who thus despise the word of God will soon make it to appear, as this king did, that they hate it too, and have not only low, but ill thoughts of it. <div eID="gen17988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17989" type="x-p"/> II. That he had not patience to hear it read through as the princes had, but, when he had heard <hi type="italic">three or four leaves</hi> read, in a rage he <hi type="italic">cut it with his penknife,</hi> and threw it piece by piece <hi type="italic">into the fire,</hi> that he might be sure to see it <hi type="italic">all consumed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.36.22-Jer.36.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. This was a piece of as daring impiety as a man could lightly be guilty of, and a most impudent affront to the God of heaven, whose message this was. 1. Thus he showed his impatience of reproof; being resolved to persist in sin, he would by no means bear to be told of his faults. 2. Thus he showed his indignation at Baruch and Jeremiah; he would have cut them in pieces, and burnt them, if he had had them in his reach, when he was in this passion. 3. Thus he expressed an abstinent resolution never to comply with the designs and intentions of the warnings given him; he will do what he will, whatever God by his prophets says to the contrary. 4. Thus he foolishly hoped to defeat the threatenings denounced against him, as if God knew not how to execute the sentence when the roll was gone in which it was written. 5. Thus he thought he had effectually provided that the things contained in this roll should spread no further, which was the care of the chief priests concerning the gospel, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.17">Acts iv. 17</reference>. They had told him how this roll had been read to the people and to the princes. "But," says he, "I will take a course that shall prevent its being read any more." See what an enmity there is against God in the carnal mind, and wonder at the patience of God, that he bears with such indignities done to him. <div eID="gen17989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17990" type="x-p"/> III. That neither the king himself nor any of his princes were at all affected with the word: <hi type="italic">They were not afraid</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.24">v. 24</reference>), no, not those princes that <hi type="italic">trembled at the word</hi> when they heard it the first time, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.16">v. 16</reference>. So soon, so easily, do good impressions wear off. They showed some concern till they saw how light the king made of it, and then they shook off all that concern. They <hi type="italic">rent not their garments,</hi> as Josiah, this Jehoiakim's own father, did when he had the <hi type="italic">book of the law</hi> read to him, though it was not so particular as the contents of this roll were, nor so immediately adapted to the present posture of affairs. <div eID="gen17990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17991" type="x-p"/> IV. That there were three of the princes who had so much sense and grace left as to interpose for the preventing of the burning of the roll, but in vain, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.25">v. 25</reference>. If they had from the first shown themselves, as they ought to have done, affected with the word, perhaps they might have brought the king to a better mind and have persuaded him to bear it patiently; but frequently those that will not do the good they should put it out of their own power to do the good they would. <div eID="gen17991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17992" type="x-p"/> V. That Jehoiakim, when he had thus in effect burnt God's warrant by which he was arrested, as it were in a way of revenge, now that he thought he had got the better, signed a warrant for the apprehending of Jeremiah and Baruch, God's ministers (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.26">v. 26</reference>): <hi type="italic">But the Lord hid them.</hi> The princes bade them abscond (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.19">v. 19</reference>), but it was neither the princes' care for them nor theirs for themselves that secured them; it was under the divine protection that they were safe. Note, God will find out a shelter for his people, though their persecutors be ever so industrious to get them into their power, till their hour be come; nay, and then he will himself be their hiding place. <div eID="gen17992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17993" type="x-p"/> VI. That Jeremiah had orders and instructions to write in another roll the same words that were written in the roll which Jehoiakim had burnt, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.27-Jer.36.28">v. 27, 28</reference>. Note, Though the attempts of hell against the word of God are very daring, yet not one iota or tittle of it shall fall to the ground, nor shall the unbelief of man make the word of God of no effect. Enemies may prevail to burn many a Bible, but they cannot abolish the word of God, can neither extirpate it nor defeat the accomplishment of it. Though the tables of the law were broken, they were renewed again; and so out of the ashes of the roll that was burnt arose another Phoenix. <hi type="italic">The word of the Lord endures for ever.</hi> <div eID="gen17993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17994" type="x-p"/> VII. That the king of Judah, though a king, was severely reckoned with by the King of kings for this indignity done to the written word. God noticed what it was in the roll that Jehoiakim took so much offense at. Jehoiakim was angry because it was <hi type="italic">written therein, saying,</hi> Surely <hi type="italic">the king of Babylon shall come and destroy this land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.36.29">v. 29</reference>. And did not <hi type="italic">the king of Babylon</hi> come two years before this, and go far towards <hi type="italic">the destroying of this land?</hi> He did so (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.6-2Chr.36.7">2 Chron. xxxvi. 6, 7</reference>) in his third year, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1">Dan. i. 1</reference>. So that God and his prophets had <hi type="italic">therefore become his enemies because they told him the truth,</hi> told him of the desolation that was coming, but at the same time putting him into a fair way to prevent it. But, if this be the thing he takes so much amiss, let him know, 1. That the wrath of God shall come upon him and his family, in the first place, by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar. He shall be cut off, and in a few weeks his son shall be dethroned, and exchange his royal robes for prison-garments, so that <hi type="italic">he shall have none to sit upon the throne of David;</hi> the glory of that illustrious house shall be eclipsed, and die in him; <hi type="italic">his dead body</hi> shall lie unburied, or, which comes all to one, <hi type="italic">he shall be buried with the burial of an ass,</hi> that is, thrown into the next ditch; it shall lie exposed to all weathers, <hi type="italic">heat and frost,</hi> which will occasion its putrefying and becoming loathsome the sooner. "Not that his body" (says Mr. Gataker) "could be sensible of such usage, or himself, being deceased, of aught that should befal his body; but that the king's body in such a condition should be a hideous spectacle, and a horrid monument of God's heavy wrath and indignation against him, unto all that should behold it." Even <hi type="italic">his seed and his servants</hi> shall fare the worse for their relation to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.31">v. 31</reference>), for they shall be punished, not for his iniquity, but so much the sooner for their own. 2. That all the evil pronounced against Judah and Jerusalem in that roll shall be brought upon them. Though the copy be burnt, the original remains in the divine counsel, which shall again be copied out after another manner in bloody characters. Note, There is no escaping God's judgments by struggling with them. <hi type="italic">Who ever hardened his heart against God, and prospered?</hi> <div eID="gen17994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17995" type="x-p"/> VIII. That, when the roll was written anew, <hi type="italic">there were added</hi> to the former <hi type="italic">many like words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.32">v. 32</reference>), many more threatenings of wrath and vengeance; for, since they will yet <hi type="italic">walk contrary to God,</hi> he will <hi type="italic">heat the furnace seven times hotter.</hi> Note, As God is in one mind, and none can turn him, so he has still more arrows in his quiver; and those who contend with God's woes do but prepare for themselves heavier of the same kind.  <chapter eID="Jer.36"/> <div eID="gen17995" type="x-p"/>

entries.b6e633f7a9454dfce7d974cc8b6facd48d1afc3b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10382"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 36</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.36.1-Jer.36.32">Jr 36:1-32</reference>. Baruch Writes, and Reads Publicly Jeremiah's Prophecies Collected in a Volume. The Roll Is Burnt by Jehoiakim, and Written Again by Baruch at Jeremiah's Dictation.</title> <div sID="gen18520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10382"/><hi type="bold">1. fourth year--</hi>The command to write the roll was given in the fourth year, but it was not read publicly till the fifth year. As Isaiah subjoined to his predictions a history of events confirming his prophecies (Is 36:1-22; 37:1-38; 38:1-22; 39:1-8), so Jeremiah also in the thirty-seventh through forty-third chapters; but he prefaces his history with the narrative of an incident that occurred some time ago, showing that he, not only by word, but in writing, and that twice, had testified all that he about to state as having subsequently come to pass [Grotius]. At the end of Jehoiakim's third year, Nebuchadnezzar enrolled an army against Jerusalem and took it in the end of the fifth or beginning of the sixth year, carrying away captive Jehoiakim, Daniel, &c. Jehoiakim returned the same year, and for three years was tributary: then he withheld tribute. Nebuchadnezzar returned and took Jerusalem, and carried off Jehoiakim, who died on the road. This harmonizes this chapter with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1-2Kgs.24.20">2Ki 24:1-20</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.1.1-Dan.1.21">Da 1:1-21</reference>. See on <reference osisRef="Jer.22.19">Jr 22:19</reference>. <div eID="gen18520" type="x-p"/>
entries.22ed48d35f531f732e399781a9d317cb800dcea4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10383"/><div sID="gen18521" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10383"/><hi type="bold">2. roll of a book--</hi>a book formed of prepared skins made into a roll. Compare "volume of the book," that is, the Pentateuch (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Psa 40:7</reference>). It does not follow that his prophecies were not before committed to writing; what is implied is, they were now written together in one volume, so as to be read continuously to the Jews in the temple.<div eID="gen18521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against ... nations--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.25.15">Jr 25:15</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen18522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from ... days of Josiah--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.25.3">Jr 25:3</reference>). From Josiah's thirteenth year (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.2">Jr 1:2</reference>). <div eID="gen18523" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7e4f01f980917fce766ad73518582282fd0fec7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10384"/><div sID="gen18524" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10384"/><hi type="bold">3. hear--</hi>consider seriously.<div eID="gen18524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return ... from ... evil way--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jonah.3.8">Jon 3:8</reference>). <div eID="gen18525" type="x-p"/>
entries.f986ae20aa72129bade4e6119815183f9f71b8f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10385"/><div sID="gen18526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10385"/><hi type="bold">4. all ... words of ... Lord--</hi>God specially suggesting what might otherwise have escaped his memory, and directing the choice of words, as well as the substance (<reference osisRef="John.14.26">Joh 14:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.16.13">16:13</reference>). <div eID="gen18526" type="x-p"/>
entries.3cc1740dd70243448c24f853ca2f8d165f0aa164: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10386"/><div sID="gen18527" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10386"/><hi type="bold">5. I am shut up--</hi>not in prison, for there is no account of his imprisonment under Jehoiakim, and <reference osisRef="Jer.36.19">Jr 36:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.26">26</reference> are inconsistent with it: but, "I am prevented," namely, by some hindrance; or, through fear of the king, to whose anger Baruch was less exposed, as not being the author of the prophecy. <div eID="gen18527" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0e40c23bc7be655040453317fe6b965a5cc20d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10387"/><div sID="gen18528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10387"/><hi type="bold">6. go--</hi>on the following year (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">Jr 36:9</reference>).<div eID="gen18528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fasting day--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">Jr 36:9</reference>). An extraordinary fast, in the ninth month (whereas the fast on the great day of atonement was on the tenth day of the seventh month, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.29">Le 16:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.27-Lev.23.32">23:27-32</reference>), appointed to avert the impending calamity, when it was feared Nebuchadnezzar, having in the year before (that is, the fourth of Jehoiakim), smitten Pharaoh-necho at Carchemish, would attack Judea, as the ally of Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.34">2Ki 23:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.35">35</reference>). The fast was likely to be an occasion on which Jeremiah would find the Jews more softened, as well as a larger number of them met together. <div eID="gen18529" type="x-p"/>
entries.77514ff924886defff566206e230bc2174218c40: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10388"/><div sID="gen18530" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10388"/><hi type="bold">7. present ... supplication--</hi>literally, "supplication shall fall"; alluding to the prostrate attitude of the supplicants (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.25">De 9:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.39">Mt 26:39</reference>), as petitioners fall at the feet of a king in the East. So Hebrew, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.26">Jr 38:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.18">Da 9:18</reference>, Margin. <div eID="gen18530" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6abfd2a5c25b361970d7bd1debde9ff528ebcbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10389"/><div sID="gen18531" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10389"/><hi type="bold">9. they proclaimed ... to all the people ... to all, &c.--</hi>rather, "all the people ... all the people proclaimed a fast" [Michaelis]. The chiefs appointed the fast by the wish of the people. In either version the ungodly king had no share in appointing the fast. <div eID="gen18531" type="x-p"/>
entries.8da0856885083795934f05ae131ca2a4a64a44cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10390"/><div sID="gen18532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10390"/><hi type="bold">10. chamber--</hi>Baruch read from the window or balcony of the chamber looking into the court where the people were assembled. However, some of the chambers were large enough to contain a considerable number (<reference osisRef="Neh.13.5">Ne 13:5</reference>).<div eID="gen18532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Gemariah--</hi>distinct from the Gemariah, son of Hilkiah, in <reference osisRef="Jer.29.3">Jr 29:3</reference>.<div eID="gen18533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shaphan--</hi>the same person as in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.3">2Ki 22:3</reference>.<div eID="gen18534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scribe--</hi>secretary of state, or he who presided over the public records.<div eID="gen18535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">higher court--</hi>that of the priests, the court of the people being lower (<reference osisRef="2Chr.4.9">2Ch 4:9</reference>).<div eID="gen18536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18537" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new gate--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.26.10">Jr 26:10</reference>). The east gate. <div eID="gen18537" type="x-p"/>
entries.bea09ce78487b8df866521a1e0ee31785ae16807: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10391"/><div sID="gen18538" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10391"/><hi type="bold">12. scribe's chamber--</hi>an apartment in the palace occupied by the secretary of state.<div eID="gen18538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">princes--</hi>holding a counsel of state at the time.<div eID="gen18539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Elnathan--</hi>who had already been an instrument of evil in Jehoiakim's hand (<reference osisRef="Jer.26.22">Jr 26:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.26.23">23</reference>).<div eID="gen18540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hananiah--</hi>the false prophet (<reference osisRef="Jer.28.10-Jer.28.17">Jr 28:10-17</reference>). <div eID="gen18541" type="x-p"/>
entries.f691f8ecbadd6ec47db361a20cf7ebb97d554c28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10392"/><div sID="gen18542" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10392"/><hi type="bold">14. Jehudi--</hi>of a good family, as appears from his pedigree being given so fully, but in a subordinate position.<div eID="gen18542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come--</hi>Instead of requiring Baruch to come to them, they ought to have gone to the temple, and there professed their penitence. But pride forbade it [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18543" type="x-p"/>
entries.85f92316416139b371ed1e4e1336f090237ce1a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10393"/><div sID="gen18544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10393"/><hi type="bold">16. afraid, both one and other--</hi>Hebrew, "fear-stricken," they turned to one another (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.42.28">Ge 42:28</reference>). This showed, on their part, hesitancy, and some degree of fear of God, but not enough to make them willing to sacrifice the favor of an earthly king.<div eID="gen18544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">We will surely tell the king--</hi>not the language of threatening but implying that the matter is of such moment that the king ought to be made acquainted with it, so as to seek some remedy against the divine anger. <div eID="gen18545" type="x-p"/>
entries.3fb0af4c76812efd84a5075587626a7768781ee4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10394"/><div sID="gen18546" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10394"/>17. What they wished to know was, whether what Baruch had read to them was written by him from memory after hearing Jeremiah repeating his prophecies continuously, or accurately from the prophet's own dictation. <div eID="gen18546" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ab0560bb8ab1eaa6a4279ec1b8885adee22f858: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10395"/><div sID="gen18547" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10395"/><hi type="bold">18. his mouth--</hi>Baruch replies it was by the oral dictation of the prophet; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.2">Jr 36:2</reference> accords with this view, rather than with the notion that Jeremiah repeated his prophecies from manuscripts.<div eID="gen18547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ink--</hi>his specification of the "ink" implies: I added nothing save the hand, pen, and ink. <div eID="gen18548" type="x-p"/>
entries.012ded029bd4121b04a109487d2e5c5b1ea2fe03: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10396"/><div sID="gen18549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10396"/>19. Showing that they were not altogether without better feelings (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.36.16">Jr 36:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.25">25</reference>). <div eID="gen18549" type="x-p"/>
entries.cbe7c8d0de7db0d1b8e25c49545ef782ac05c54d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10397"/><div sID="gen18550" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10397"/><hi type="bold">20. chamber--</hi>There were chambers in the king's palace round the court or great hall, as in the temple (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.10">Jr 36:10</reference>). The roll was "laid up" there for safekeeping, with other public records. <div eID="gen18550" type="x-p"/>
entries.d13f4d99173264a0d1bf3c993c36a8a82af03189: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10398"/><div sID="gen18551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10398"/><hi type="bold">21. sent Jehudi--</hi>Note how unbelievers flee from God, and yet seek Him through some kind of involuntary impulse [Calvin]. Jehudi seems to have been the king's ready tool for evil. <div eID="gen18551" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fd8d1184214611cf8ab9915de54cbfa0d6bdfd7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10399"/><div sID="gen18552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10399"/><hi type="bold">22. winter house--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">Am 3:15</reference>).<div eID="gen18552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ninth month--</hi>namely, of the religious year, that is, November or December.<div eID="gen18553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18554" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire on ... hearth--</hi>rather, the stove was burning before him. In the East neither chimneys nor ovens are used, but, in cold weather, a brazen vessel containing burning charcoal; when the wood has burned to embers, a cover is placed over the pot to make it retain the heat. <div eID="gen18554" type="x-p"/>
entries.b63d0d0956f63d9694f64308b007c1e2b15b5f76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10400"/><div sID="gen18555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10400"/><hi type="bold">23. three or four leaves--</hi>not distinct leaves as in a book, but the consecutive spaces on the long roll in the shape of doors (whence the Hebrew name is derived), into which the writing is divided: as the books of Moses in the synagogue in the present day are written in a long parchment rolled round a stick, the writing divided into columns, like pages.<div eID="gen18555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pen-knife--</hi>the writer's knife with which the reed, used as a pen, was mended. "He" refers to the king (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.22">Jr 36:22</reference>). As often as Jehudi read three or four columns, the king cut asunder the part of the roll read; and so he treated the whole, until all the parts read consecutively were cut and burnt; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.24">Jr 36:24</reference>, "all these words," implies that the whole volume was read through, not merely the first three or four columns (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.8">1Ki 22:8</reference>). <div eID="gen18556" type="x-p"/>
entries.3ba3a04226140c698399896950d2570d28e37571: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10401"/><div sID="gen18557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10401"/>24. The king and his "servants" were more hardened than the "princes" and councillors (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.36.12">Jr 36:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.14">Jr 36:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.36.16">Jr 36:16</reference>). Contrast the humble fear exhibited by Josiah at the reading of the law (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.11">2Ki 22:11</reference>). <div eID="gen18557" type="x-p"/>
entries.11f3fabcdb0ac8c4934041449b100632bc96913a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10402"/><div sID="gen18558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10402"/>25. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.36.16">Jr 36:16</reference>). The "nevertheless" aggravates the king's sin; though God would have drawn him back through their intercession, he persisted: judicial blindness and reprobation! <div eID="gen18558" type="x-p"/>
entries.670a8706fb4e85a084e68455a0293df6b076a093: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10403"/><div sID="gen18559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10403"/><hi type="bold">26. Hammelech--</hi>not as Margin, "of the king." Jehoiakim at this time (the fifth year of his reign) had no grown-up son: Jeconiah, his successor, was then a boy of eleven (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.36">2Ki 23:36</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.8">2Ki 24:8</reference>).<div eID="gen18559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hid them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.31.20">Psa 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.83.3">83:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.20">Is 26:20</reference>). <div eID="gen18560" type="x-p"/>
entries.389287f2cbd38b3406996f02d46e0bde000258f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10404"/><div sID="gen18561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10404"/><hi type="bold">27. roll, and ... words--</hi>that is, the roll of words. <div eID="gen18561" type="x-p"/>
entries.d99862b281db29cd12b3c7c4774577a1cd3943d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10405"/><div sID="gen18562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10405"/><hi type="bold">28. all the former words--</hi>It is in vain that the ungodly resist the power of Jehovah: not one of His words shall fall to the ground (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.18">Mt 5:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.5">Ac 9:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.39">5:39</reference>). <div eID="gen18562" type="x-p"/>
entries.39d9b37c8c4da0c1cf98cd6e594224aa4f20eaa7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10406"/><div sID="gen18563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10406"/><hi type="bold">29. say to Jehoiakim--</hi>not in person, as Jeremiah was "hidden" (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.26">Jr 36:26</reference>), but by the written word of prophecy.<div eID="gen18563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, Why--</hi>This is what the king had desired to be said to Jeremiah if he should be found; kings often dislike the truth to be told them. <div eID="gen18564" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e2d5792a153cd2f4d011edeae9cdcf0c6cfcc53: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10407"/><div sID="gen18565" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10407"/><hi type="bold">30. He shall have none to sit upon the throne--</hi>fulfilled (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.8">2Ki 24:8</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1-2Kgs.25.30">2Ki 25:1-30</reference>). He had successors, but not directly of his posterity, except his son Jeconiah, whose three months' reign is counted as nothing. Zedekiah was not the son, but the uncle of Jeconiah, and was raised to the throne in contempt of him and his father Jehoiakim (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.30">Jr 22:30</reference>).<div eID="gen18565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18566" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dead body ... cast out--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.22.18">Jr 22:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.19">19</reference>).<div eID="gen18566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day ... heat ... night ... frost--</hi>There are often these variations of temperature in the East between night and day (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.40">Ge 31:40</reference>). <div eID="gen18567" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c2b9a67aa1274abc2cf2c4c46f23a3b0e3f0853: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10408"/><div sID="gen18568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10408"/><hi type="bold">32. added besides ... many like words--</hi>Sinners gain nothing but additional punishment by setting aside the word of Jehovah. The law was similarly rewritten after the first tables had been broken owing to Israel's idolatry (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.19">Ex 32:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.1">34:1</reference>). <chapter eID="Jer.36"/>

entries.4f2954828562ffd3220d8d803de63319253ac4e2: <div eID="gen30311" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30312" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30313" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30313" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30312" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30314" type="x-p"/> God commands Jeremiah to write down in one roll or volume all the predictions he had uttered against Israel and Judah, and all the surrounding nations, from the day of his vocation to the prophetic office, that the house of Judah might have abundant warning of the dreadful calamities with which their country was about to be visited, if not prevented by a timely repentance, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.1-Jer.36.3">Jer 36:1-3</reference>. The prophet employs Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, to write from his mouth all the words of the Lord, and then to read them publicly upon a fast day in the Lord's house, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.4-Jer.36.8">Jer 36:4-8</reference>. A general fast is proclaimed in the following year, viz., the fifth year of the reign of Jehoiakim; upon which occasion Baruch, in obedience to the prophet's command, reads the words of Jeremiah to all the people at the entry of the new gate of the temple, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">Jer 36:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.10">Jer 36:10</reference>. The princes, hearing of this, send for Baruch, who reads the roll to them; at the contents of which they are greatly alarmed, and solemnly resolve to give information to the king, at the same time advising both the prophet and his scribe to hide themselves, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.11-Jer.36.19">Jer 36:11-19</reference>. Jehoiakim likewise having sent for the roll, Jehudi reads to him a part; and then the king, though advised to the contrary by some of has princes, having cut the leaves, throws the whole into the fire, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.20-Jer.36.25">Jer 36:20-25</reference>, and orders Jeremiah and Baruch to be seized; but they could not be found, because a special providence of God had concealed them, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.26">Jer 36:26</reference>. Jeremiah is commanded to re-write his prophecies, and to denounce the judgments of God against the king who had destroyed the first roll, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.27-Jer.36.31">Jer 36:27-31</reference>. Baruch accordingly writes from the mouth of Jeremiah a new copy, with numerous additions, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.32">Jer 36:32</reference>. <div eID="gen30314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30315" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30316" type="x-p"/> And it came to pass in the fourth year - About the end of this year, see <reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">Jer 36:9</reference>. This discourse also bears its own date, and was probably delivered at a time when the people enjoyed peace, and were about to celebrate one of their annual fasts.
entries.dc23bf71d8ea32dcc37840cdc1fa001274617864: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen30316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30317" type="x-p"/> Take thee a roll of a book - Take a sufficient quantity of parchment; cut and stitch it together, that it may make a roll on which to write the words that I have already spoken, that they may serve for a testimony to future generations. The Jewish rolls, several of which now lie before me, were made of vellum, or of sheep-skins dressed in the half-tanned or Basil manner. These were cut into certain lengths, and those parts were all stitched together, and rolled upon a roller. The matter was written on these skins in columns or pages. Sometimes two rollers are used, that as the matter is read from the roll in the left hand, the reader may coil it on the roller in his right. In this form the Pentateuch is written which is read in the synagogues.
entries.d116989f85f545d2555e771795823fdb473e2669: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30318" type="x-p"/> It may be that the house of Judah will hear - It was yet possible to avert the judgments which had been so often denounced against them. But in order to this they must - <div eID="gen30318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30319" type="x-p"/> 1. Hear what God has spoken. <div eID="gen30319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30320" type="x-p"/> 2. Every man turn from his evil way. <div eID="gen30320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30321" type="x-p"/> 3. If they do so, God graciously promises to forgive their iniquity and their sin.
entries.3f6aedea3246b3f6b33b4c0dbc0105bd0cbe14d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen30321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30322" type="x-p"/> Then Jeremiah called Baruch - This man, so useful to the prophet, and so faithfully attached to him, was by office a scribe; which signifies, not only a writer, but also a man in office; a chancellor, secretary, etc., a learned man; one acquainted with laws and customs.
entries.d18b2bebec65fb100a177dc9c8e3667e02f72d23: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen30322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30323" type="x-p"/> Upon the fasting day - A day when multitudes of people would be gathered together from all parts to implore the mercy of God. This was a favorable time to read these tremendous prophecies.
entries.366d2bb9041c0a7162a864c04cab80fa096da427: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30324" type="x-p"/> Present their supplication - "Let their supplication fall," that they may fall down before God, and deplore their sins.
entries.d82c6a72c629ac42349842acdad8da5cef0d722f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen30324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30325" type="x-p"/> In the ninth month - Answering to a part of our December.
entries.75063da224a5779f86f01937c63829ebeb7aab91: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen30325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30326" type="x-p"/> In the chamber of Gemariah - He was one of the princes of Judah. See <reference osisRef="Jer.36.12">Jer 36:12</reference>.
entries.cfcb05df757055939693dded7060d835b1605c22: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen30326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30327" type="x-p"/> How didst thou write all these words? - At his mouth? - So the text should be pointed. They wished to know whether he had not copied them, or whether he wrote as Jeremiah prophesied.
entries.83945c36d86541a78f313a65e982031b96f9a7b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30328" type="x-p"/> Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah - They saw that the king would be displeased, and most probably seek their lives; and as they believed the prophecy was from God, they wished to save both the prophet and his scribe; but they were obliged to inform the king of what they had heard.
entries.aefa614feae6dc667e40852cffdf203a9d6bb10d: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30329" type="x-p"/> Winterhouse - A warm apartment suited to the season of the year, (December), when in Palestine there is often snow upon the ground, though it does not last long. A fire on the hearth - a pan or brazier of burning coals. This is the case to the present day. In cold weather the rich burn wood in brass or earthen pans, placed in any part of the room; the indigent burn sticks on the floor.
entries.598729207bf82c7d6aa61d1fd2d13eafa4796cbb: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen30329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30330" type="x-p"/> When Jehudi had read three or four leaves - Rather columns; for the law, and the sacred Hebrew Books, are written in columns of a certain breadth. דלתות delathoth, signifies gates or openings between column and column, or between section and section. <div eID="gen30330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30331" type="x-p"/> He cut it with the penknife - בתער הספר bethaar hassopher, "the knife of the scribe," properly enough penknife. <div eID="gen30331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30332" type="x-p"/> And cast it into the fire - To show his contempt for God's words.
entries.26576dc64a35e27e5d59014fc1811a12aab95316: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen30332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30333" type="x-p"/> Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah - Three of the princes wished to save the roll, and entreated the king that it might not be burnt. They would have saved it out of the fire, but the king would not permit it to be done.
entries.ea73bb8e1e16cd4d4efeb57edcd55a436831121c: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen30333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30334" type="x-p"/> But the Lord hid them - They had, at the counsel of some of the princes hidden themselves, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.19">Jer 36:19</reference>. And now, though a diligent search was made, the Lord did not permit them to be found.
entries.2191deeecae6ff9ba67294bd8ac4bfaf9fea1d00: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen30334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30335" type="x-p"/> Take thee again another roll - There was no duplicate of the former preserved; and now God inspired the prophet with the same matter that he had given him before; and there is to be added the heavy judgment that is to fall on Jehoiakim and his courtiers.
entries.b22488bf322b2cfffb0a93579ce9e2d343addb4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen30335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30336" type="x-p"/> He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David - He shall have no successor and himself shall have an untimely end, and shall not even be buried, but his body be exposed to the open air, both night and day. He who wishes to hide his crimes, or take away the evidence which is against him, adds thereby to his iniquities, and is sure in consequence to double his punishment. See the threatening against Jehoiakim, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.19">Jer 22:19</reference> (note), and the note there.
entries.7f977716e0b54db071364ac9aae96e6be314d21f: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen30336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30337" type="x-p"/> There were added - many like words - All the first roll, with many other threatening and perhaps more minute declarations which were merely of a temporary importance and local application; and the Holy Spirit did not think proper to record them here.  <chapter eID="Jer.36"/> <div eID="gen30337" type="x-p"/>

entries.ba069508ca843de3f84d399be56612372c3e2c0c: <reference osisRef="Jer.36.1">Jer 36:1</reference> <div eID="gen14271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14272" type="x-p"/> In the fourth year of the reign of Jehoiakim the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, bidding him commit to writing all the addresses he had previously delivered, that Judah might, if it were possible, still regard the threatenings and return (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.1-Jer.36.3">Jer 36:1-3</reference>). In accordance with this command, he got all the words of the Lord written down in a book by his attendant Baruch, with the further instruction that this should be read on the fast-day in the temple to the people who came out of the country into Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.4-Jer.36.8">Jer 36:4-8</reference>). When, after this, in the ninth month of the fifth year of Jehoiakim, a fast was appointed, Baruch read the prophecies to the assembled people in the chamber of Gemariah in the temple. Michaiah the son of Gemariah mentioned the matter to the princes who were assembled in the royal palace; these then sent for Baruch with the roll, and made him read it to them. But they were so frightened by what was read to them that they deemed it necessary to inform the king regarding it (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.9-Jer.36.19">Jer 36:9-19</reference>). At their advice, the king had the roll brought and some of it read before him; but scarcely had some few columns been read, when he cut the roll into pieces and threw them into the pan of coals burning in the room, at the same time commanding that Baruch and Jeremiah should be brought to him; but God hid them (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.20-Jer.36.26">Jer 36:20-26</reference>). After this roll had been burnt, the Lord commanded the prophet to get all his words written on a new roll, and to predict an ignominious fate for King Jehoiakim; whereupon Jeremiah once more dictated his addresses to Baruch (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.27-Jer.36.32">Jer 36:27-32</reference>). <div eID="gen14272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14273" type="x-p"/> Since Jeremiah, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.36.3">Jer 36:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.6">Jer 36:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.7">Jer 36:7</reference>, is to get his addresses written down that Baruch may be able to read them publicly on the fast-day, now at hand, because he himself was prevented from getting to the temple, the intention of the divine command was not to make the prophet put down in writing and gather together all the addresses he had hitherto given, but the writing down is merely to serve as a means of once more presenting to the people the whole contents of his prophecies, in order to induce them, wherever it was possible, to return to the Lord. In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar, after vanquishing the Egyptians at the Euphrates, advanced against Judah, took Jerusalem, and made Jehoiakim tributary. In the same year, too, Jeremiah had delivered the prophecy regarding the giving up of Judah and all nations for seventy years into the power of the king of Babylon (Jer 25); ); this was before he had been bidden write down all his addresses. For, that he did not receive this command till towards the end of the fourth year, may be gathered with certainty from the fact that the public reading of the addresses, after they were written down, was to take place on the fast-day, which, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">Jer 36:9</reference>, was not held till the ninth month of the fifth year. The only doubtful point is, whether they were written down and read before or after the first capture of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. Most modern commentators take the former view; e.g., Hitzig says, briefly and decidedly, "According to <reference osisRef="Jer.36.29">Jer 36:29</reference>, the Chaldeans had not as yet appeared in the country." But this is not mentioned in Jer 36:29. The threatening in this verse, "The king of Babylon shall come and destroy this land, and exterminate men and beasts from it," does not prove that the king of Babylon had not yet come to Judah, but merely that the country had not yet been destroyed, and men and cattle exterminated from it. When Jerusalem was first taken, Nebuchadnezzar contented himself with subjecting Jehoiakim under his supreme authority and requiring the payment of tribute, as well as carrying away some of the vessels of the temple and some hostages. The devastation of Judah and the extirpation of men and beasts did not commence till the second subjugation of Jerusalem under Jehoiakim, and was completed when the city was utterly destroyed, in Zedekiah’s time, on its third subjugation. The settlement of the question that has been raised depends on the determination of the object for which the special fast-day in the fifth year was appointed, whether for averting the threatened invasion by the Chaldeans, or as a memorial of the first capture of Jerusalem. This question we have already so far decided in the Commentary on <hi type="italic">Daniel</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Jer.1.1">Jer 1:1</reference>, where it is stated that the fast was held in remembrance of that day in the year when Jerusalem was taken for the first time by Nebuchadnezzar; we have also remarked in the same place, that Jehoiakim either appointed or permitted this special fast "for the purpose of rousing the popular feeling against the Chaldeans, to whom they were in subjection, - to evoke in the people a religious enthusiasm in favour of resistance; for Jehoiakim keenly felt the subjugation by the Chaldeans, and from the first thought of revolt." However, every form of resistance to the king of Babylon could only issue in the ruin of Judah. Accordingly, Jeremiah made Baruch read his prophecies publicly to the people assembled in the temple on that day, "by way of counterpoise to the king’s desire;" the prophet also bade him announce to the king that the king of Babylon would come, i.e., return, to destroy the land, and to root out of it both men and beasts. These circumstances give the first complete explanation of the terror of the princes when they listened to the reading of the book (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.16">Jer 36:16</reference>), as well as of the wrath of the king, exhibited by his cutting the book in pieces and throwing it into the fire: he saw that the addresses of the prophet were more calculated to damp those religious aspirations of the people on which he based his hopes, than to rouse the nation against continued submission to the Chaldeans. Not till now, too, when the object of the appointment of the fast-day was perceived, did the command given by God to the prophet to write down his prophecies appear in its proper light. Shortly before, and in the most earnest manner, Jeremiah had reminded the people of their opposition to the word of God preached by him for twenty-three years, and had announced to them, as a punishment, the seventy years’ subjugation to the Chaldeans and the desolation of the country; yet this announcement of the fearful chastisement had made no deeper or more lasting impression on the people. Hence, so long as the threatened judgment was still in the distance, not much could be expected to result from the reading of his addresses in the temple on the fast-day, so that the command of God to do so should appear quite justified. But the matter took a considerably different from when Nebuchadnezzar had actually taken Jerusalem and Jehoiakim had submitted. The commencement of the judgments which had been threatened by God was the proper moment for laying before the hearts of the people, once more, the intense earnestness of the divine message, and for urging them to deeper penitence. Just at this point the reading of the whole contents of the prophecies delivered by Jeremiah appears like a final attempt to preserve the people, on whom judgment has fallen, from complete destruction.
entries.d8cad0e74201894df8ec6101ef599463e0b5e681: <reference osisRef="Jer.36.2-Jer.36.3">Jer 36:2-3</reference> <div eID="gen14273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14274" type="x-p"/> The word of the Lord to Jeremiah was to this effect: <hi type="italic">"Take thee a book-roll, and write on it</hi> (אליה for עליה) <hi type="italic">all the words that I have spoken unto thee concerning Israel and Judah, and concerning all the nations, from the day I spake unto thee, from the days of Josiah till this day. </hi> Jer 36:3. <hi type="italic">Perhaps the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I meditate doing to them, that they may return every one from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin."</hi> ישׁמעוּ here means, to hear correctly and lay to heart; cf. Jer 26:3. Hitzig views the command as meaning, not that Jeremiah is now for the first time to write down his addresses (which would be an impossibility for the most faithful memory), but that he is merely to write them down together in one book, out of the several scattered leaves and scraps. Graf has already refuted this view, though more fully than was necessary. It is not a copying, word for word, of every separate address that is meant, but merely a writing down of the essential contents of all his oral discourses. This is quite clear, not merely from what is stated in <reference osisRef="Jer.36.3">Jer 36:3</reference> as the object of this command, but also from the character of these collected addresses, as they are preserved to us. That the expression "all the words" is not to be understood in the most rigid sense, follows from the very fact that, when Jeremiah anew wrote down his prophecies, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.32">Jer 36:32</reference>, he further added "many similar words" to what had been contained in the first book-roll, which was burned by Jehoiakim. But Jeremiah might perhaps be able to retain in his memory the substance of all the addresses he had delivered during the twenty-three years, since all of them treated of the same subjects - reproof of prevailing sins, threat of punishment, and promises.
entries.27ddf0325e236bae16ef23cf45afbd07ed9828d1: <reference osisRef="Jer.36.4-Jer.36.7">Jer 36:4-7</reference> <div eID="gen14274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14275" type="x-p"/> Jeremiah carries out the divine command by making Baruch write down on a book-roll all the words of the Lord, out of his mouth ('מפּי , i.e., at the dictation of Jeremiah); and since he himself is prevented from getting to the house of the Lord, he bids him read the words he had written down in the ears of the people in the temple on the fast-day, at the same time expressing the hope, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.7">Jer 36:7</reference> : "Perhaps their supplication will fall down before the Lord, and they will return each one from his wicked way; for great is the wrath and the anger which the Lord hath expressed concerning this people." Baruch, who is mentioned so early as Jer 32:12. as the attendant of the prophet, was, according to the passage now before us, his amanuensis, and executed his commissions. אני עצוּר, according to <reference osisRef="Jer.33.1">Jer 33:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.39.15">Jer 39:15</reference>, might mean, "I am in prison;" but this does not accord with the request of the princes, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.19">Jer 36:19</reference>, that Jeremiah should hide himself. Moreover, עצוּר does not mean "seized, <hi type="italic">captus</hi>," but "stopped, restrained, hindered;" see on Neh 6:10. The cause of hindrance is not mentioned, as being away from the purpose of the narrative. "To read in the roll in the ears of the people," i.e., to read to the people out of the book. בּיום צום does not mean "on any fast-day whatever," but, "on the fast-day." The article is omitted because there was no need for defining the fast-day more exactly. The special fast-day mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.36.9">Jer 36:9</reference> is intended. 'תּפּל תּחנּתם וגו, "their supplication will fall down before the Lord," i.e., reach unto God, as if it were laid before His feet. נפל is transferred from the posture of the suppliant - his falling down before God - to his supplication. Hence, in Hiphil, to make the supplication fall down before the Lord is equivalent to laying the request at His feet; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.26">Jer 38:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.42.9">Jer 42:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.18">Dan 9:18</reference>, Dan 9:20. If the supplication actually comes before God, it is also heard and finds success. This success is pointed out in 'וישׁבוּ וגו, "that they may repent." If man, in a repentant spirit, supplicates God for grace, God grants him power for conversion. But the return of the people from their wicked way is indispensable, because the wrath which God has expressed concerning it is great, i.e., because God has threatened a heavy judgment of wrath.
entries.a4643fb843eb78c4b0874d9b139ce94553030b9a: <reference osisRef="Jer.36.8">Jer 36:8</reference> <div eID="gen14275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14276" type="x-p"/> Baruch executes his commission.
entries.1000a97aadc26aa05d30cfd8ff1ff3713d219421: <reference osisRef="Jer.36.9-Jer.36.19">Jer 36:9-19</reference> <hi type="italic">The reading of the book in the temple.</hi> - Jer 36:9. In the fifth year of Jehoiakim, in the ninth month, <hi type="italic">"they proclaimed a fast before the Lord - all the people in Jerusalem, and all the people who had come out of the cities of the Judah to Jerusalem."</hi> קתא צום, <hi type="italic">to call, declare, appoint a fast</hi>; cf. 1Ki 21:9, 1Ki 21:12; 2Ch 20:3. From the tenor of the words, the people who lived in Jerusalem and those who had come thither out of the country might seem to have called the fast. But this is impossible; for the people from the cities of Judah evidently came to Jerusalem only in consequence of the fast being appointed. Hence Graf is of opinion that קתא צום seems here used in a general way of the keeping of such a fast. This view is not confirmed by any parallel instances. The expression is inexact, and the inexactness has arisen from the effort to attain greater conciseness of expression. The meaning is this: a fast was proclaimed, and all the people in Jerusalem and out of the cities of Judah came to worship the Lord in the temple. It remains doubtful with whom the appointment originated, - whether with the king, or with the high priest and the priesthood. The ninth month corresponds to our December, and consequently came round with the cold season; cf. Jer 36:22. The fast-day was a special one; for in the law only the day of atonement, in the seventh month, was prescribed as a fast-day. On the object of this measure, see <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 316f.
entries.1f914fd2dbc289e1126273a516832578b3525a9f: <reference osisRef="Jer.36.20">Jer 36:20</reference> <hi type="italic">The reading of the book before the king</hi>. - Jer 36:20.
