He says that the dead body of Jehoiakim would be cast out, to be exposed to the cold in the night, and to the heat in the day This might seem unimportant, like what we threaten children with, when we mention some phantoms to them; for what harm could it have been to Jehoiakim to have his dead body exposed to the cold in the night? for no injury or feeling of sorrow can happen to a dead body, as a dead man as to his body can have no feeling. It seems then that it is to little purpose that the Prophet says, that his dead body would be exposed to the heat in the day, and to the cold at night. But this is to be referred to the common law of nature, of which we have spoken elsewhere; for it is a sad and disgraceful thing, nay, a horrid spectacle, when we see men unburied; and the duty of burying the dead has from the beginning been acknowledged, and burial is an evidence of a future resurrection, as it has been before stated. When, therefore, the body of man lies unburied, all men shun and dread the sight; and then when the body gets rigid through cold, and becomes putrid through the heat of the day, the indignity becomes still greater. God then intended to set forth the degradation that awaited Jehoiakim, not that any hurt could be done to him when his body was cast out, and not honored with a burial, but that it would be an evidence of God’s vengeance, when a king was thus cast out as an ass or a dog, according to what we have seen elsewhere, “With the burial of an ass shall he be buried,” that is, he will be deemed unworthy of common honor; for as it falls to the lot of the lowest of men to find a pit where their bodies lie buried, it was a rare and unusual proof of God’s vengeance, that a king should he exposed as a prey to birds and wild beasts. We know what Jehu said of Jezebel,
“Let her be buried, for she is a king’s daughter.” (2 Kings 9:34)
She was worthy to be torn to pieces a hundred times. She had been cast out from a chamber, and the dogs licked her blood; yet an enemy ordered her to be buried — and why? because she was a king’s daughter, or descended from a royal family, (1 Kings 21:23:) then, he said, let her be buried.
We now then understand the meaning of the Prophet, or rather of the Holy Spirit, that it would be a remarkable proof of God’s vengeance, when the body of King Jehoialdm should be exposed at night to the cold, and in the day to the heat. This has also happened sometimes to the saints, as we have before said; but it was a temporal punishment common to the good and to the bad. We ought yet always to consider it as God’s judgment. When a godly man is left without burial, we must know that all things happen for good to God’s children, according to what Paul says, whether it be life or death, it is for their salvation. (Romans 8:28) But when God gives a remarkable proof of his wrath against an ungodly man, our eyes ought to be opened; for it is not right to be blind to the manifest judgments of God; for it is not in vain that Paul reminds us that God’s judgment will come on the ungodly; but he would have us carefully to consider how God punishes the reprobate in life and in death and even after death. It follows —
Jeremiah 36:31
31. And I will punish him and his seed and his servants for their iniquity; and I will bring upon them, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and upon the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them; but they hearkened not.
31. Et visitabo super eum et super semen ejus, et super servos ejus iniquitatem eormn, et evenire faciam illis (super eos, ad verbum) et super habitatores Jerusalem, et super virum Jehudab omne malum quod pronuntiavi adversus cos, et non a udierunt.
entries.7793047eb85ab073eda9bd45005f14eae63c5f8e:
Here a reason is given for what the former verse contains; for if the Prophet had only said, that the dead body of the king would remain unburied and cast out in dishonor to be exposed in the night to the cold and in the day to the heat, the narrative would not have produced the effect intended; but God shews here the cause, which was this, that he had forewarned King Jehoiakim and all his counsellors, (called here servants) and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and all the Jews universally: as then they had been in due time clearly told what calamity was near at hand, and yet no one had repented, for this so great an obstinacy God says now that he would take vengeance, I will visit him and his seed and the whole people for their iniquity — what was the iniquity? even that they had so grievously and in so many ways provoked God, and had not returned to a sound mind, though reproved by the Prophet, but had become more and more hardened.
The extremity of their iniquity the Prophet thus points out, because they hearkened not to the threatenings, by which God had endeavored to rescue them from the coming ruin: for there would have been some hope of deliverance, had they deprecated God’s wrath; but as his threatenings had been despised, it was, as I have said, an extreme iniquity. And we see elsewhere how much God abominates this diabolical presumption of men,
“I have called to sackcloth and ashes; but ye have called to the harp and to joy, and have said, ‘Let us feast and drink, for to-morrow we shall die:’ as I live, this iniquity shall not be blotted out.” (Isaiah 22:12, 13)
God swore by himself, that this sin should not be expiated, for the Jews repented not when he kindly invited them to himself, and declared to them that they could not escape extreme punishment. It is therefore no wonder that God in this place also represents their obstinate wickedness as being the greatest, the Jews having not hearkened to the reproofs conveyed to them by the mouth of Jeremiah. It follows —
Jeremiah 36:32
32. Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burnt in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words.
32. Et (tunc) Jeremias scripsit volumen aliud, et dedit Baruch filio Neriae, qui scripsit in ipso ex ore Jeremiae cunctos sermones libri, quem combusserat Joiakim rex Jehudah igne, et adhuc additi sunt cum illis sermones multi similes illis.
entries.ae6fc0b36283b3078402026416bddaa3e74acad3:
Here the Prophet tells us that he faithfully obeyed God in writing another volume; and his constancy in this affair deserves no common praise; for he had lately fled in fear, he knew that the king was his enemy, as he had already ordered him and Baruch to be slain. As then he knew that the king burned with so much rage and hatred, how came he to be so bold as to exasperate him still more? But we see that the Prophets were not exempt from the influence of fear, and were often anxious about their own safety; and yet they ever preferred the duty imposed on them by God to their own life. The Prophet, no doubt, trembled, but as he felt bound to obey God’s command, he disregarded his own life, when he had to make the choice, whether to refuse the burden laid on him, or to provide for his own safety. Thus then he offered his own life as a sacrifice, though he was not free from fear and other infirmities. This is one thing.
But Baruch, I doubt not, again proclaimed these words; how was it then that the king abstained from cruelty? Had his madness been by any means mitigated? It is certain that he did not become changed, and that he did not through kindness spare God’s servants; but God restrained his cruelty; for when it is not his will to soften the hearts of the ungodly, he yet bridles their violence, so that they either dare not, or cannot find the way, to execute with their hands what they have intended in their minds, however much they may strive to do so. I therefore consider that the King Jehoiakim was restrained by the hidden power of God, so that he could not do any harm to Jeremiah and his scribe Baruch; and that in the meantime the magnanimity of the Prophet and also of his scribe remained invincible; for it was God’s will to fight as it were hand to hand, with this impious king, until he was ignominiously cast from his throne, which happened, as we shall see, soon after.
PRAYER
Grant, Omnipotent God, that since thou warnest us by so remarkable examples, that the ungodly by obstinately resisting thee, do nothing but aggravate their own ruin, — O grant, that we may receive with meek hearts the admonitions of thy Prophets, and submit to thee, and be so humbled by thy threatenings and tremble at thy word, that being touched with the feeling of true repentance, and reconciled to thee by faith, we may find thee to be the best and the kindest Father to obedient children, until we shall at length enjoy that eternal inheritance which has been obtained for us by the blood of thine only-begotten Son. — Amen.
Lecture One Hundred and Forty-Fifth
CHAPTER 37
Jeremiah 37:1-2
1. And king Zedekiah the son of Josiah reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, whom Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah.
1. Et regnavit rex Zedechias, filius Josiae, pro Choniah (Jechania) filio Joiakim, quem constituit regem Nebuchadnezer, rex Babylonis, in terra Jehudah:
2. But neither he, nor his servants, nor the people of the land, did hearken unto the words of the LORD, which he spake by the prophet Jeremiah.
2. Et non audivit, neque servi ejus, neque populus terrae sermones Jehovae, quos loquutus est per manum Jeremiae Prophetae.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="36" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. XXXVI.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 AND it came to pass in the fourth year of Jehojakim, the son of Josiah king of Judah, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> this word came unto Jeremi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ah, from the LORD, saying <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Iehojakim</ns0:hi> was three years a Tributary to <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar,</ns0:hi> as we read, 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 24.1. then he rebelled, which three years are judged to be the 6, 7, and 8 years of his Reign, for <ns0:hi>Pharaoh Necho</ns0:hi> set him up, to whom he was first a Tributary as we read 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 23.35. <ns0:hi>Pharaoh Necho</ns0:hi> having conquered him, <ns0:hi>Iehoja<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kim</ns0:hi> became Servant to the Conqueror 3 years, then rebelled; upon which the Armies of the <ns0:hi>Chaldaeans</ns0:hi> with the <ns0:hi>Syrians, &c.</ns0:hi> came up against him; and carried him away. This word of the Lord came to <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> the first year that he was Tributa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry to the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> which was the fourth year of his Reign.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 Take thee a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 8.1.</ns0:note> roll of a book <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">By a <ns0:hi>roll of a book</ns0:hi> is to be understood <ns0:hi>parchments,</ns0:hi> which an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciently were their books, the art of binding books being not then known.</ns0:note> and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 30.2.</ns0:note> write therein all the words that I have spoken unto thee, against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations from the day I spake unto thee, from the dayes of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 25.3.</ns0:note> Josiah even unto this day <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The precept is for recording all the Revelations he had from God for 22 years last past, for he began to pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phesie in the thirteenth year of <ns0:hi>Iosiah,</ns0:hi> who reigned one and thirty years, so as he prophesied 18 years, during <ns0:hi>Iosiah</ns0:hi>'s life, this was the fourth year of the Reign of <ns0:hi>Iehojachim.</ns0:hi> God would have them recorded, that there might be a memorial of them, that so the truth of them might appear, when God should bring them to pass, the time of which now drew very near.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil <ns0:note place="bottom">What we translate <ns0:hi>it may be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> others translate <ns0:hi>if perhaps</ns0:hi> which better expresseth the sense. God knew what would be, but yet he would not be wanting in means by which they might be informed in his will, and so believe the thing, for believing and reforming are here meant by <ns0:hi>hearing,</ns0:hi> as the next words in part expound this term here.</ns0:note> which I purpose to do unto them, that they may return every man from his evil way, that I may forgive their iniquity, and their sin <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Forgiveness of sin in Scrip<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture sometimes signifieth the acquitting of a sinner from the ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ligation sin layeth the sinner under to Eternal death, sometimes the remission of a temporal punishment, it may here well be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood as comprehending both, though I think the latter to be what is here principally intended.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riah, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 45.1.</ns0:note> Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah, all the words of the LORD, which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">We shall find this <ns0:hi>Baruch</ns0:hi> being one of <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi>'s Disciples, more than once thus imployed as <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi>'s Secretary or <ns0:hi>Ama<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nuensis.</ns0:hi> None shall need ask how <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> could remember all the prophesies he had prophesied for 22 years before past that considereth who it was that commanded him to do this. God undoubtedly revived the Prophets memory, or he could not have called all to mind.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 And Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> shut up, I cannot go into the house of the LORD.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:48" />6 Therefore go thou and read in the roll which thou hast written from my mouth, the words of the LORD in the ears of the people in the LORDS house upon the fasting day <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">We do not read that <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> was a prisoner in the fourth year of <ns0:hi>Iehoiachim,</ns0:hi> and therefore it is very incertainly guested in what sense he here saith he was <ns0:hi>shut up,</ns0:hi> some think <ns0:hi>Iehoiachim</ns0:hi> had imprisoned him, or at least restrained him to his house, tho we do not read of it. Others think he restrained himself, but in what sense he was shut up, is not certain, that he was so, is cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain, he knew that God had not commanded his prophecies to be written for any other end, but that the people might have them recalled to their memories, he being not in a capacity himself at present to speak any thing to the people in so pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lick a place, sendeth <ns0:hi>Baruch</ns0:hi> to do it in his stead, chusing for it a day of publick Fast, not the day of the yearly fast mentioned, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 23.2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. But on a fast day (of which we shall read more, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 9.) proclaimed by <ns0:hi>Ieho<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>achim,</ns0:hi> probably to avert the ven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />geance hanging over them from the <ns0:hi>Chaldaeans,</ns0:hi> or rather from the drought. It was undoubtedly because of the concourse of people which the Prophet knew would that day be in the Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple that he chose that day, when some would be present from all parts of <ns0:hi>Iudah.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>: and also thou shalt read them in the ears of all Judah, that come out of their Cities.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 It may be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>their sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plication shall <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>all.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> they will present their supplica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion before the LORD, and will return every one from his evil way, for great is the anger, and the fury, that the LORD hath pronounced against this people <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">We had an expression like this, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 3. it teacheth us that the only means to turn away God's fierce anger ready to fall upon people is Prayer and Reformation.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And Baruch the son of Neriah, did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book the words of the LORD, in the LORDS house.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And it came to pass in the fifth year of Jeho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />iachim, the son of Josiah king of Judah, in the ninth moneth, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> they proclaimed a fast before the LORD to all the people in Jerusalem, and to all the people that came from the Cities of Judah unto Jerusalem.<ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This fast was appointed upon a particular emergency, whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther it was for a Famine which was then in the Land, or to avert the ruine which they justly feared from the king of <ns0:hi>Baby<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lon,</ns0:hi> who had lately brought them under his servitude is not cer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain; the yearly fast, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 23.27. was to be kept in the se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venth moneth, nor did God ever ordain any fast to be kept in the ninth moneth.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Then read Baruch in the book the words of Jeremiah in the house of the LORD, in the cham<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan the scribe, in the higher court, at the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 26.10.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>door.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> entry of the new gate, of the LORDS house in the ears of all the people <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This verse only attesteth <ns0:hi>Baruch</ns0:hi>'s obedience to the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand of the Prophet <ns0:hi>Ieremy</ns0:hi> not only as to the thing, his reading it in the Temple, but as to the circumstance in as publick a man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner as he could in <ns0:hi>the chamber of Gemariah, &c.</ns0:hi> most likely out of some window, or in some <ns0:hi>Balcony,</ns0:hi> the people being below, and hearing it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan had heard out of the book all the words of the LORD.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Then he went down into the kings house, into the scribes chamber, and lo all the princes sate there, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Ach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Ze<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">It is uncertain whether this <ns0:hi>Micajah</ns0:hi> went to make this Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation to the Princes who sate in the Secretaries Chamber, as a piece of news only, or out of a malitious design to accuse the Prophet, and <ns0:hi>Baruch</ns0:hi> for what was done as a seditious pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Then Micajah declared unto them all the words that he had heard when Baruch read the book in the ears of the people <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">That is, the substance of all the words, for none can ima<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gine that an hearer could remember every word, which shews the vanity of those who overstrain such universal particles to signifie every particular word or person.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 Therefore all the princes <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">That is, all the Princes that at that time sate there in Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cel, sent a messenger with a command to <ns0:hi>Baruch</ns0:hi> to appear before them, and to bring the roll which he had read in the Ears of the people.</ns0:note> sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah the son of Cushi unto Baruch, saying, Take in thy hand the roll, wherein thou hast read in the ears of the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, and come. So Baruch the son of Neriah, took the roll in his hand, and came unto them <ns0:hi>o.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">And they said unto him, Sit down now, and and read it in our ears, So Baruch read <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> in their ears <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The courage of <ns0:hi>Baruch</ns0:hi> is admirable, he was now before the Councel, in the Kings house, the substance of the Prophe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cies, were threatning both to the King, and Court, and to all the people. The King as appears by all history, was of no good temper, we read <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 26. <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 23. of his sending for <ns0:hi>Vrijah</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Prophet</ns0:hi> out of <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> when he had <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>led thither for fear of the King, and slaying him, and we shall find that at this time, the Princes advised both <ns0:hi>Ieremy</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Baruch</ns0:hi> to hide themselves, yet <ns0:hi>Baruch</ns0:hi> is not afraid, but reads the Prophecy in their Ears.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 Now it came to pass, when they had heard all the words, they were afraid both one and other <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">It is hardly to be imagined that all these Counsellors should sit still till they had heard all <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi>'s prophecies for 22 years read, but <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> signifies many, or the sence and substance of all the prophecies.</ns0:note>, and said to Baruch, we will surely tell the king of all these words <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">They were all of them afraid, <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> had now been above twenty years a Prophet to this people, and doubtless in great esteem for 18 years of it, while <ns0:hi>Iosiah</ns0:hi> was alive, and one whose prophecies they could not but observe had been oft accomplished, therefore they could not but be afraid that they should see these words also fulfilled, and took them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves bound in duty to acquaint the King with them. Some if not all of these probab y had been great men in <ns0:hi>Iosiah</ns0:hi>'s time, which was but four or five years before, and from him sucked in some good and religious principles which begat some aw of God in them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And they asked Baruch, saying, Tell us now, How didst thou write all these words at his mouth <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This now seemed but a reasonable question, considering they were the substance of what he had been prophecying for so many years. The thing seemed strange to the Princes, Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets being not used to study and pen their discourses, but to speak them <ns0:hi>extempore.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 Then Baruch answered them, He pronoun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ced all these words unto me with his mouth, and I wrote them with <ns0:hi>ink</ns0:hi> in the book <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">This could not but add to the Princes fear and amazement. They must needs conceive that the thing was done from God, for without a special influence of God, it had been a thing impossible, that <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> should have called to mind all that he had spoken at several times in so many years, and proceeding from the God of truth, they must needs fear, that they would have their certain and just accomplishment in their season.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Then said the Princes unto Baruch, Go, hide thee, thou, and Jeremiah, and let no man know where ye be <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This speaketh these Princes to have been men, of a much gentler temper, and better disposition, than those who succeed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed them in <ns0:hi>Zedekiah</ns0:hi>'s time, they were not willing that any harm should come to the Prophet, nor to <ns0:hi>Baruch,</ns0:hi> and knew the fierce temper of <ns0:hi>Iehojachim,</ns0:hi> and therefore advised <ns0:hi>Baruch,</ns0:hi> that both he, and the Prophet should hide themselves.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And they went in to the king, into the court, but they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, and told all the words in the ears of the king <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">They were obliged by their Office as Councellors to the King, to acquaint him with what they heard, which might be prejudicial to him, and his Nation, and indeed this was the very end, why God had commanded the enrolling of these Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phecies, that both the King, and Princes, and People might take notice of them, but they did not carry the book with them, but laid it up in the Secretaries Chamber.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 So the king sent Jehudi to set the roll, And he took it out of Elishama the scribes chamber, And Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes which stood beside the king <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">It appeareth by <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. that this <ns0:hi>Iehudi</ns0:hi> was a Messenger commonly imployed by the king, and Councel, him the <ns0:hi>King</ns0:hi> sends to fetch the <ns0:hi>Roll</ns0:hi> (before called a book) then he imploy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth him to read it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:48" />22 Now the king sate in the winter-house in the ninth moneth, and <ns0:hi>there was a fire</ns0:hi> on the hearth burning before him <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The ninth moneth with them, answered part of our <ns0:hi>No<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vember</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>December,</ns0:hi> which was a time of the year called for fires.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">And it came to pass <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">That is the king, not having patience to hear above three or four collumns, or periods, or titles took the pen-knife, that (it is like) <ns0:hi>I<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>hudi</ns0:hi> had, and cut it in pieces, and burned it in the fire that was before him, not considering that it was the Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />velation of the will of God, but exalting himself above all that was called God. This shewed both the wickedness, and passio<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nate temper of this Prince, and his high contempt of God and his Prophets.</ns0:note> cut it with the pen-knife, and cast <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> into the fire, that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> on the hearth.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Yet they were not afraid, nor <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 King<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 22.11.</ns0:note> rent their garments, <ns0:hi>neither</ns0:hi> the king nor any of his servants that heard all these words <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">So hardned were this peoples hearts that though they knew that <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> was a Prophet of the Lord, upon the expe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rience now of more than twenty years, and the whole scope of his prophecies had been to denounce the just Judgments of God, that now were coming upon this people, and they could not but understand, that God must be greatly assistant to <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> in writing this <ns0:hi>Roll</ns0:hi>; all the matter of which he could not other<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wise have kept in mind so many years, yet they had no serious fear of God upon their hearts working upon the hearing the dreadful matter of these prophecies, nor shewed any sign of re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />morse, or sense of their sins, or God's Judgments coming upon them as indications of his wrath.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 Nevertheless Elnathan, and Delaiah, and Gemariah, had made intercession to the king, that he would not burn the roll, but he would not hear them <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">These three Princes seemed to have had a greater dread of God upon their hearts than the rest, for so far as they durst, they interposed, and besought the King not to burn the Roll, but he would not hearken to their advice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 But the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>of the King.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Hammelech and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe, and Jeremiah the prophet <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The King was not satisfied with burning the Roll, but gives order to apprehend both <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Baruch,</ns0:hi> and commandeth the three persons named in this verse to do it:</ns0:note>: But the LORD hid them <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">But God by his providence kept them both out of their hands; how the Lord hid them we are not told, the Princes (as we read before) advised <ns0:hi>Baruch</ns0:hi> that they should both hide themselves. This Phrase (probably) imports no more, than that God directed them to find such a place of recess as the Kings messengers could by no means find out, nor understand where they were, till the King's passion was a little over.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Then the word of the LORD came to Je<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />remiah after that the king had burnt the roll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah saying,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll which Jehojakim the king of Judah hath burnt.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And thou shalt say to Jehojakim, king of Ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dah, Thus saith the LORD, Thou hast burnt this roll, saying, Why hast thou written therein, saying, The king of Babylon shall certainly come, and destroy this land, and shall cause to cease from thence man and beast <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">It speaketh nothing but the impotency, and passion, and debauchery of humane Nature to swell against any Revelations of the Divine Will, the Counsels of the Lord shall stand, and men only further entangle themselves by strugling in the Lords net. <ns0:hi>Iehojakim</ns0:hi> burns one Roll, God will have the same thing wrote in another.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">We learn here both what was the matter of <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi>'s prophecy, and the cause of the Kings anger he had prophecyed that the King of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> should come, take <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and lay the countrey waste, which as to <ns0:hi>Iehojachim</ns0:hi>'s part, was fulfilled within six years after this, more fully in 18 years, but corrupt Princes can endure nothing that shall make their lives uneasie.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 Therefore thus saith the LORD of Jehoja<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kim the king of Judah, He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That is, none that shall be King any considerable time, <ns0:hi>Ie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />coniah,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Iehojachin</ns0:hi> his son was set up, but kept his Throne but three moneths. 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 24.8, 9, 10.</ns0:note>, and his dead body shall be <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">chap. 22.19.</ns0:note> cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">We no where read of the time, or manner of this Kings Death, but that he had an ignominious Burial, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 22.19. like the Burial of an <ns0:hi>Ass</ns0:hi>; none accompanying his Corps, none mourning for him, and it appears from this Text, that wherever he dyed, his Body lay for a time unburied.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And I will <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>visit up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> punish him, and his seed, and his servants, for their iniquity, and I will bring upon them, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lem, and upon the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them, but they heark<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned not <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">As to the people God threatneth, they should feel, what they were not willing to hear, even all the evil which God by his Prophet had pronounced against them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch, the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book, which Jehojakim the king of Judah, had burnt in the fire, and there were ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ded besides unto them many <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>as they.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> like words <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Wicked men get nothing by opposing themselves to the revealed will of God, how ungrateful soever it be to them, but the addition of guilt to their souls, and the increase of Divine Wrath, God's counsels shall stand, and what he speaks shall most certainly be accomplished. Here is another roll written with additional threatnings confirmative of what God had before said.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
